transcript.content: Hello, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

I guess… what finally made me come in is that I don’t feel much like myself anymore. The part of me that used to reach for people, or feel really engaged in my work, has just gotten very quiet.

I used to enjoy yoga, and going to galleries, and journaling—actually I have this one notebook I bought at a museum shop that I thought would make me write every day, but it just sits there. Mostly I’m just moving through obligations now, doing what has to be done, but not really… feeling connected to it.
Have you been feeling down or depressed?

I don’t know if I’d call it depressed exactly… maybe. It’s more like everything in me got muted. Like, the part of me that used to want to call someone, or get excited about a case at work, or go to yoga after a long day—that part’s just gone quiet.

Even things I used to really like, like galleries or journaling… I have this notebook I bought because it was so beautiful, and I thought, “This will make me write again,” but it just sits there. So I’m still doing what I’m supposed to do, mostly, but it feels like I’m just moving through obligations rather than actually feeling much from them.
Did this start after something stressful happened in your life?

Yeah… I think it did kind of line up with something. We took my older relative into our apartment about eight months ago, and since then this whole shift has been happening—how I think, how I work, how I talk to people.

I mean, I don’t want to blame them, because that feels unfair, and there were a lot of little adjustments, like where things go in the kitchen and schedules and… you know, just the whole apartment feeling different. But if I’m being honest, that’s around when I started noticing I wasn’t really myself anymore.
Over the past couple of weeks, have you been feeling sad or down most days?

I’m not sure I’d say “sad” exactly… not most days in that clear way, like crying or feeling heartbroken. It’s more hard for me to name. Some days I’ll sit there and realize I’ve been staring at the same mug or email for too long, but then I think, well, everyone does that, don’t they?

So… I don’t know. Maybe down, but not in a way I can put a clean label on.
Lately, have you been having trouble concentrating?

Concentrating… I mean, I’m not sure. I notice it more when someone asks me directly, because then I start thinking about whether I’m thinking properly, which is a little funny, I guess.

At work I still get through things, but sometimes I’ll read the same line more than once and then wonder if it’s the wording or just me. But then forms are written badly half the time anyway, you know? So I don’t know if I’d call it “trouble concentrating” exactly. Maybe just… slower to settle into something.
Do you still enjoy the things you used to, like yoga, galleries, or journaling?

I used to, yeah. Yoga especially was sort of… I don’t know, it kept me tethered. And galleries, I’d make a whole afternoon of it, even if I only liked one piece, and then I’d write about it later.

Lately it’s like that part of me has gone very quiet. I still do what I’m supposed to do—work things, errands, answering people—but I don’t really reach for any of it the way I used to. Even journaling feels like an obligation, and that’s strange because it used to be where I put everything. That’s kind of what finally made me come in, honestly.
Over the last two weeks, have you felt down or empty for most of the day on nearly every day?

Nearly every day… I don’t know. That sounds so definite, and I get stuck on the wording. “Empty” is a funny word, because sometimes I’ll feel sort of blank, but then I’ll remember I still made dinner or answered a message, so maybe that doesn’t count?

Most of the day, nearly every day… I’m not sure I could honestly say that. It’s been off and on, more like I notice something isn’t quite right, and then I get distracted by what I need to do. I’m sorry, I know that’s not a clean yes or no.
Has this been making it hard for you to function at work or take care of things at home?

I’m still showing up, so in that sense I’m functioning. I mean, I get dressed, I go in, I answer emails—mostly. Home is… not perfect, but it’s not like everything has collapsed.

Work is where it’s more noticeable, I think. I’ve missed a couple of grant deadlines, which is not really like me. I used to be the person reminding everyone else about those things. And my supervisor hasn’t made a big announcement or anything, but she’s quietly shifted some of my more demanding clients to other clinicians. She said it was to “balance the caseload,” which… maybe it is, but I know what that usually means.

So yes, I guess it is affecting things. Not catastrophically, but I’m not at my usual level.
When you’re away from home and not around your relative, do you feel more like yourself?

I’m not sure I’ve really noticed it that cleanly. Like, if I’m at work I can sort of slip into the role, you know, because there are expectations and a schedule, and that can make me seem more like myself from the outside.

But “feel more like myself” is harder. Sometimes being away from home is a relief just because there are fewer little household things pulling at me—laundry, dishes, the pile of mail that somehow becomes symbolic, which sounds silly. My aunt used to call it “paper clutter,” and she had this whole system with colored folders… sorry, that’s not really what you asked.

I guess I don’t have a clear yes or no. I haven’t paid attention to whether it changes specifically when I’m away from my relative. It might, but I’d have to think about it more.
When your relative is away and you have the apartment to yourself, do you feel more like yourself?

I don’t know that I’ve tracked it that way. When I’m alone in the apartment, sometimes it feels quieter, and I can move things around or leave a cup somewhere without feeling like it means something. But then I also get aware of the quiet, and I start noticing all the things I should probably be doing.

“More like myself” is hard to pin down. I keep thinking of how I used to really like having an empty afternoon at home, like with tea and a book, but now I mostly think about whether I’m using the time correctly, which is probably not what you meant. So… I’m not sure. I don’t have a clear answer.
Have you been waking up earlier than usual and unable to fall back asleep?

I’m not sure. I don’t think I’ve been keeping track of the exact time I wake up, which I probably should if we’re talking about sleep. Sometimes I wake and look at the clock, but then I start thinking about whether the clock is too bright—my mother used to put a scarf over hers, which seems like a fire hazard now that I say it.

But earlier than usual and can’t fall back asleep… I don’t know. I can’t give you a clean yes or no.
Have you had thoughts that life isn’t worth living?

I… I’m not sure how to answer that exactly. I mean, “worth living” feels like such a big phrase, and I start thinking about whether people mean it literally or more like when you’re exhausted and everything feels pointless for a bit.

I’ve definitely had times where I wonder what I’m doing, like if I’m spending my day right, or if I’ve let things get too… stalled. My old supervisor used to say social workers are terrible at applying things to themselves, which is funny and not funny. But I don’t know if that’s what you’re asking.

So I guess I don’t have a clear answer right now. I’d need you to maybe ask it a different way.
Have you had thoughts about wanting to be dead?

I don’t know. “Wanting to be dead” sounds very definite, and I’m not sure I can say that. Sometimes I get caught on the wording, because there’s wanting something and then there’s just feeling tired of having to keep sorting things out, and those aren’t exactly the same.

I remember in school they made us practice asking questions like this plainly, and it always felt easier on the other side of the clipboard. Not that there’s a clipboard now, I just mean… I’m having trouble giving you a straight yes or no.
Have you had moments when you wished you could go to sleep and not wake up?

I don’t know that I’ve had it in that exact way. Like, sleep sometimes sounds very appealing, but that’s true for a lot of people, isn’t it? My aunt used to say sleep was “the poor person’s vacation,” which I always thought was kind of grim and funny at the same time.

But wishing I wouldn’t wake up… I’m not sure. I don’t want to say yes if that makes it sound more specific than it is. I get tangled up in the wording. I think I’d need to sit with that for a minute.
In the past two weeks, have you wished you could go to sleep and not wake up?

In the past two weeks… I’m still not sure I can pin that down cleanly. I’ve had nights where I wanted to just stop thinking and sleep for a long time, but “not wake up” feels like a different sentence, if that makes sense.

I keep thinking about how people use phrases loosely, like “I could sleep forever,” and then in this room it means something much more exact. So… I don’t know that I’ve wished that, not in a clear way. I’m having trouble giving you a yes or no.
Over the past two weeks, have you been feeling tired or low on energy most days?

I’m not sure. I mean, I get tired sometimes, but “most days” is where I start counting and then I lose the thread. Energy is a funny word too, because people say it like it’s a battery, but I’ve never really felt like that’s how it works.

Some days I feel worn out, but I don’t know if it’s enough to call it most days. I haven’t really been keeping track.
Before your relative moved in eight months ago, did you already feel this way for a long time?

Before that? No, not really in the same way. I mean, I’ve always had periods where work felt heavy—social work can do that, you know, people think it’s all paperwork but it gets in your bones sometimes—but this particular change, the way my thinking and work and even talking to people has felt different… that’s been more like eight months.

It started around when we took my older relative into our apartment. Or, not started like a light switch, but that’s the marker I keep coming back to. Before that, I don’t think it had been going on for a long time.
Before your relative moved in, was there ever another period in your life when, for at least two weeks, you lost interest in things you usually enjoy?

Before they moved in… I’m trying to think. I don’t know if I’d call it a whole separate period like that.

What brought me in now is more that the part of me that used to naturally reach for people, or feel something from work, or yoga, or going to galleries, even journaling… it’s all gotten very quiet. I still do some things because they’re obligations, or because I’m supposed to, but it feels like I’m mostly just moving through them.

Before then, I had low patches, sure, like anyone, but I don’t remember another clear two-week stretch where I lost interest in everything the way this feels now.
Right now, do things outside of work still feel enjoyable to you?

Not really, no. I mean, I still go through the motions with some things outside work—like yoga, or I’ll think about going to a gallery, and I used to journal a lot—but it’s like the part of me that would actually feel pulled toward those things has gone quiet.

I still do what I’m supposed to do, or what’s already on the calendar, but it feels more like checking something off than enjoying it. Even reaching out to people feels… farther away than it used to.
Since your relative moved in, have you been feeling anxious or on edge?

Anxious or on edge… I don’t know. I mean, I wouldn’t say that’s the main thing I notice.

It’s been tense having another person in the apartment, just logistically—like where things go, who’s using the kitchen, all of that—but I don’t know if that’s “anxious” exactly. Sometimes I feel kind of wound up, but then I start thinking maybe anyone would, with that kind of change. So… I’m not sure how to answer that cleanly.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether there has ever been a prolonged baseline of chronic low mood/anhedonia predating the recent stressor, to distinguish adjustment disorder or single depressive episode from persistent/recurrent depressive conditions.
doctor.question: Before your relative moved in eight months ago, did you already feel this way for a long time?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This whole change in how I’m thinking, working, and connecting with people has been going on for about eight months, since we took my older relative into our apartment.

patient.answer:
Before that? No, not really in the same way. I mean, I’ve always had periods where work felt heavy—social work can do that, you know, people think it’s all paperwork but it gets in your bones sometimes—but this particular change, the way my thinking and work and even talking to people has felt different… that’s been more like eight months.

It started around when we took my older relative into our apartment. Or, not started like a light switch, but that’s the marker I keep coming back to. Before that, I don’t think it had been going on for a long time.

inference.note: Ruled out F34.1 because symptoms were not present for a long duration before the stressor; current picture remains most consistent with an adjustment-related depressive/anxious syndrome, with depressive disorder, recurrent depression, anxiety disorder, and burnout still in the differential due to limited endorsement of full major depressive criteria.

doctor.question: Before your relative moved in, was there ever another period in your life when, for at least two weeks, you lost interest in things you usually enjoy?

patient.answer:
Before they moved in… I’m trying to think. I don’t know if I’d call it a whole separate period like that.

What brought me in now is more that the part of me that used to naturally reach for people, or feel something from work, or yoga, or going to galleries, even journaling… it’s all gotten very quiet. I still do some things because they’re obligations, or because I’m supposed to, but it feels like I’m mostly just moving through them.

Before then, I had low patches, sure, like anyone, but I don’t remember another clear two-week stretch where I lost interest in everything the way this feels now.

doctor.intent: Differentiate depression/adjustment disorder from burnout or nonspecific anxiety by clarifying whether the loss of interest extends beyond work into other parts of life.
doctor.question: Right now, do things outside of work still feel enjoyable to you?

target_item.name: Negative_Symptoms
target_item.manifestation: What finally brought me in is that I feel like the part of me that used to reach for people and take pleasure in my work, yoga, galleries, even journaling, has gone very quiet, and I’m mostly just moving through obligations.

patient.answer:
Not really, no. I mean, I still go through the motions with some things outside work—like yoga, or I’ll think about going to a gallery, and I used to journal a lot—but it’s like the part of me that would actually feel pulled toward those things has gone quiet.

I still do what I’m supposed to do, or what’s already on the calendar, but it feels more like checking something off than enjoying it. Even reaching out to people feels… farther away than it used to.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the symptoms are occurring in the context of a stressor without meeting criteria for a major depressive episode, by assessing excessive worry/anxiety as the distinguishing feature for adjustment disorder with mixed anxiety and depressed mood versus depressive disorder or burnout.

patient.answer:
Anxious or on edge… I don’t know. I mean, I wouldn’t say that’s the main thing I notice.

It’s been tense having another person in the apartment, just logistically—like where things go, who’s using the kitchen, all of that—but I don’t know if that’s “anxious” exactly. Sometimes I feel kind of wound up, but then I start thinking maybe anyone would, with that kind of change. So… I’m not sure how to answer that cleanly.

Full criteria for a major depressive episode were not clearly established: the patient repeatedly denied or could not confirm persistent depressed mood, neurovegetative symptoms, or suicidal ideation. Anxiety symptoms were not prominent enough for a primary anxiety disorder. Burnout alone does not account for the broader mood/interest changes linked to the home stressor.
